title: Why Willpower Isn’t Enough To Improve Self-Control—and What Works Instead
summary: How society misunderstands willpower and how mindfullness practice can help.
body:
The Misconception

People proficient in self-control are often seen as having a high level of willpower. They are imagined as gladiators forging the path forward, no matter the resistance. Their good behavior is labeled as self-discipline, while those who struggle to cultivate positive habits are labeled as lazy or unmotivated, which often becomes internalized. While the willpower approach can work for some, in many ways it is antithetical to the way the brain works.  This article will dispel some common misconceptions surrounding self-control and lay out a new model of self-control more aligned with the brain's natural processes, so that you do not have to wage war every day just to get on the treadmill or make it to work on time. 

What doesn’t get talked about

What the willpower approach misses about self-control is that, evolutionarily, our brains are often meant to respond to things automatically for our survival. For example, when people get dangerously cut off in traffic, many have the unconscious response of road rage. This is so common that we may not think twice upon experiencing it, but intellectually, this response is illogical. We understand that driving is relatively safe, people make mistakes, and that while the event was scary or aggravating, it is over and we need to continue driving as safely as possible. So why the reaction? Many of these reactions involve neural systems that evolved long before the uniquely human capacity for complex conscious reasoning. Structures including the brainstem and basal ganglia play important roles in regulating automatic behaviors, movement, motivation, and responses to environmental cues. Albeit necessary, these automatic responses often conflict with the goals set by our rational mind. For example, when we are energized and conscious, we may want to diet, but when driving home exhausted from work, the mind sees McDonald's as an opportunity to gain energy without much work. 

Combating these automatic responses becomes increasingly difficult once they are ingrained as a habit. Once a behavior is repeated often enough to be a habit, cues (people, places, things, etc.) can trigger the performance of said habit. Not only can these cues trigger somatic feedback, but they also trigger thoughts of what the habitual response should be. For example, runners who ran consistently automatically brought to mind thoughts of running and jogging when exposed to words associated with the environments in which they regularly run (Neal et al., 2012). 

Intention alone is not enough to break these habits. Research has found that intention is a stronger predictor of action when the action is performed infrequently. When intentions waver, behavior usually falls back to the habitual baseline (Rebar et al. 2014). For example, a student who feels less motivated to study on a given day, will likely then study the amount that is regular or habitual. 

The Missing Piece: Cognitive Control

This regression to repetition can make it seem as if we are doomed to repeatedly sink to the level of our habits. Luckily for us, this is not so. Our brain has the ability to become aware of discrepancies between our behavior and our goals. Picture this situation. You want to start going to the gym after work. The next day you come home from work, sit down, open your phone, and after an hour of scrolling you retroactively realize you wasted your time. The next day you come home, pull out your phone, but then you think, “Oh, I'm doing it again. I said I was going to run.” That is conflict monitoring, the brain's ability to detect competing responses or discrepancies that may require additional control. That does not mean you have solved your problems or broken your habit, just that now you have been given a chance to redirect control for your habitual hardwiring. 

Evidence suggests that the primary mechanism monitoring this conflict is the Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) (Botnvink et al., 2001). The ACC activates in situations where there are competing responses or interference between different neural processing streams. In the context of habits, the ACC can be thought of as the commander in charge of deploying troops to the conflict. Put into application, the function of the ACC could look something like the following. Say you are trying to quit smoking. The automatic habit of smoking becomes activated due to a cue. Your new intention of not smoking introduces a competing response plan. The ACC could then detect this conflict between competing automatic and goal-directed responses. The ACC then sends a signal indicating that more control is needed, activating regions like the prefrontal cortex. Again, this does not fix your habit; it simply offers the opportunity for you to hold back the automatic response. 

The Pause: From Impulse to Choice 

So now the ACC has allowed us to pause; what should we do next? Well, the willpower model will tell you suppression is the answer. To tell yourself, " Oh, I shouldn’t be feeling this, or I should be doing that.” Once again, this idea of self-constraint is not in line with the way the brain works. At this stage of processing, we have not necessarily acted on the impulse. We have detected the conflict, creating an opportunity for cognitive control to influence what happens next. The next step then becomes awareness, noticing that you have a particular urge or automatic response. The goal is not to judge; simply observe before we automatically obey. 

This introduces the concept of response flexibility. Without awareness, habits tend to be a cycle of impulses leading to unconsciousness. Now, we know we have the ability to experience an impulse, to be aware of it, and then, after awareness has been established, we can begin to introduce competing responses. As aforementioned, situations that introduce multiple competing responses are more likely to activate the ACC, which can signal areas of the brain responsible for executive functioning, letting them know that more top-down processing is necessary. 

It is important to note that an increase in awareness does not mean the impulse goes away or that you will make the correct choice. It simply gives you flexibility by providing distance between you and your automatic responses. 

Mindfulness as the Training of Awareness

So if awareness is paramount during this critical moment following the ACC’s detection of conflict, can we get better at awareness? Let’s start with a definition. Awareness, in this context, means noticing what you are thinking, feeling, and the urges arising in your body as they are happening.

This is a particular skill we do not practice often in the modern world. Especially during situations that may trigger internal conflict, for many of us, our attention turns outward. We often focus on surviving, navigating, or masking ourselves in these situations rather than turning inward. So how can we focus on the skill of internal observation?

The answer to this question has been around for nearly as long as recorded history itself: the practice of mindfulness. A practical definition of mindfulness in this context would be the practice of intentionally bringing attention to present-moment experience with an attitude of observation rather than immediate reaction or judgment. 

It is important to note that mindfulness is not a catch-all or gold standard intervention for those who struggle with self-control. Rather, it helps train several skills that are useful throughout the self-control process. The most pertinent of these skills is Meta-Awareness. Defined as awareness of what your mind is doing while it is doing it, cultivating Meta-Awareness drastically shifts how we relate to our impulses. Regular awareness may have an observation such as “I am angry,” whereas a meta-aware thought may sound something like “I am aware that I am angry and I am aware of how my anger is affecting the situation I am in.” A simplified version of the model of self-awareness laid out thus far would look something like automatic process → conflict → monitoring → awareness → opportunity for control. Meta-Awareness helps us stay conscious that this process is happening at all. Mindfulness practice can help us train the skill of meta-awareness by sharpening our mind's ability to notice when attention goes. Take the practice of mediation for example. One focuses on their breath; their mind inevitably wanders; they notice that it wanders, and then they return to their breath. The most important part is not returning to the breath; it is the moment of noticing that you are no longer paying attention. This is an invaluable skill when the key inflection moment of self-control requires paying attention to how our impulses pull us back to habits during times of low motivation. The better we are at catching these slips in attention, the harder it is for impulses to sneak up on us. 

Another skill mindfulness helps us cultivate is decentering. Decentering is the ability to experience thoughts, emotions, and urges without automatically treating them as facts, commands, or definitions of yourself. Decentering provides an outlet for us to experience an impulse without immediately acting upon it. By developing decentering, individuals can better recognize impulsive tendencies and choose more deliberate, controlled responses, thereby enhancing self-control. Essentially, decentering allows for increased awareness of one’s internal processes, which supports managing impulses and maintaining goal-directed behavior. (Maloney et al., 2024).  

Perhaps the most concrete skill in regulating self-control that mindfulness can help cultivate is attention shifting. As aforementioned, impulses associated with habits are strongly connected to cues. If Meta-Awareness helps us notice when our attention is low, attention shifting helps us notice when our attention becomes focused on these cues and strengthens our ability to redirect to something more goal-oriented. Here we can draw a parallel between mindfulness practice and real-world implementation. The practice of noticing the breath, getting distracted, noticing the distraction, then returning to breath, is functionally similar to setting a goal, getting distracted, noticing you are distracted, and returning focus to your goal. They're obviously not the same process, but mindfulness repeatedly exercises a component of the broader process. 

Rethinking Self-Control 

We now understand that self-control emerges from the interaction between automatic processes, goals, monitoring, awareness, and cognitive control. A simplified model may look something like this (note this is not a literal sequence of brain region firing): automatic process → goal conflict → monitoring → awareness → pause → evaluation/response → behavior. This model makes it clear that the skill we need to train is not the ability to eliminate or power through our impulses. The true skill we need to cultivate is the ability to recognize when we are engaging in an automatic behavior opposed to our goals, create enough cognitive space and flexibility to pause, and then be able to redirect our attention to our goals and the behaviors that will help us get there. Mindfulness training is not the catch-all solution, and even if you are able to be mindful of what is happening, it does not mean you will always make the right choice. However, mindfulness provides necessary foundational skills for giving us a fighting chance at resisting automatic behavior.
